I have been farming in Quzhou County for over forty years, and I know our land on the North China Plain rewards careful timing. I manage seven mu of flat, irrigable fields. I will not gamble on unfamiliar crops this year. The wheat–maize double-cropping system is our family’s backbone: winter wheat gives us grain and straw for the household, and summer maize brings cash after the wheat comes off. Because I finished high school and I keep up with the county extension station’s leaflets, I pay attention to balanced fertilization and pest scouting rather than spraying by habit.

For winter wheat, I will sow an improved variety in early October. Before sowing I will run the rotary tiller to break up the stubble and level the seedbed. I will put down compound fertilizer as a basal dose and top-dress with urea at green-up and jointing. Water is the lifeline here, so I will irrigate four times: once before winter if the soil is dry, once at jointing, once at flowering, and once during grain filling. I also plan four pesticide applications—herbicide at pre-sowing, then fungicide and insecticide as needed when the weather turns humid.

For summer maize, I will direct-seed a hybrid variety with a no-till seeder the same week the wheat is harvested in early June. There is no time to waste between crops, and no-tillage saves diesel and preserves soil moisture. I will apply starter compound fertilizer with the seed. Maize needs less irrigation than wheat here, but the big trumpet stage and the tasseling stage are critical, so I will irrigate twice if the rains fail. I will spray herbicide once before sowing and watch for corn borers; three pesticide rounds in total should be enough.
